title: Event Loop
body:
JavaScript runs on a single thread, yet a page doesn't freeze while waiting on a network response. The event loop is why. Long-running work — a [[Fetch]], a timer, a click waiting to happen — is handed off to the browser's own subsystems, not to your JS thread. When that work completes, a callback is queued, and the event loop picks it up as soon as the [[Call Stack]] is empty.

So the sequence in [[Asynchronous JS]] is: synchronous code runs to completion first, then queued callbacks run. That's the actual mechanism behind a [[Promise]] resolving "later", and behind the classic surprise of `console.log` printing `undefined` immediately after a fetch. It also means one genuinely slow synchronous loop *does* block everything — the event loop grants concurrency for waiting, not parallelism for computing.
